teaser: The first free man to accept Islam. The companion in the cave. The one the Prophet called 'freed from the Fire.'
quran_mention: The second of the two, when they were in the cave — Allah says: 'Do not grieve, Allah is with us.' (9:40)

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: The man who believed without hesitation
layers.content:
His name was Abdullah ibn Abi Quhafa, whose name was Uthman ibn Amir ibn Amr ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murra. His kunya was Abu Bakr. His mother was Umm al-Khayr Salma bint Sakhr.

He was a wealthy merchant of Makka. When the Prophet was sent, Abu Bakr had forty thousand dirhams. He spent all of them freeing and strengthening the Muslims until he came to Madina with only five thousand dirhams — and there did what he used to do in Makka.

He was called al-Atiq — the freed one. The Messenger of Allah looked at him and said: 'This is one freed by Allah from the Fire.' He was also called as-Siddiq — the one who confirms the truth absolutely. When the Prophet described the Night Journey, the people rejected it. Abu Bakr said, 'If he said it, it is true.' The Prophet said: 'He is the Siddiq.'
layers.quran_ref: Quran 9:40 — 'the second of the two, when they were in the cave'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: The first free adult man to enter Islam
layers.content:
Multiple narrations confirm Abu Bakr as-Siddiq was the first free man to become Muslim. Asma bint Abi Bakr said: 'My father was the first of the Muslims to become Muslim and by Allah, I only knew my father when he was following the deen.'

Aisha, Umm al-Mu'minin, narrated: 'I did not know my parents but that they were following the deen, and no day went by but the Messenger of Allah would come to us morning and evening.'

Ibrahim an-Nakha'i said: 'Abu Bakr was called awwah — one of great compassion and mercy.' Ali ibn Abi Talib confirmed this from the minbar: 'Abu Bakr was awwah, with a repentant heart.'

When Abu Bakr became Muslim he had forty thousand dirhams. He used every dirham to free enslaved believers — Bilal, Ammar, and others — without expecting anything in return. When the Prophet mentioned this to him, Abu Bakr said: 'I have already freed him, Messenger of Allah.'
layers.hadith_ref: Reported by Asma bint Abi Bakr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The companion in the cave — second of two
layers.content:
When the command to emigrate came, the Messenger of Allah said to Abu Bakr: 'I was commanded to leave.' Abu Bakr asked: 'In company, Messenger of Allah?' He replied: 'You have company.'

They went out until they reached the cave of Thawr and concealed themselves. Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr brought news of the people of Makka by night. Amir ibn Fuhayra herded sheep and brought them milk. Asma made food and sent it with him. When she could find nothing to tie the bag, she cut her belt in two — earning her title: Dhat an-Nitaqayn, the one with two belts.

When the Messenger of Allah told Abu Bakr to lead the prayer during his final illness, Abu Bakr wept until those praying behind him could not hear his recitation. He was the only person the Prophet trusted to stand in his place before the community. Yazid ibn Harun narrated: 'The Messenger of Allah said to Abu Bakr, "I was commanded to emigrate." Abu Bakr asked, "In company?" He replied, "You have company."'
layers.quran_ref: Quran 9:40 — 'He said to his companion: Do not grieve, Allah is with us'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: As-Siddiq — the one who confirms without hesitation
layers.content:
His defining quality was immediate, unconditional confirmation of the Prophet ﷺ. When others hesitated, when evidence was demanded, when people required proof — Abu Bakr confirmed. This is what earned him the title as-Siddiq.

Yazid ibn Harun narrated: the Prophet said about the Night Journey, 'I said to Jibril: My people do not believe me.' Jibril said: 'Abu Bakr believes you. He is the Siddiq.'

Muslim al-Batin said of him: 'They freed foolishness from the wazir of their Prophet.' Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As confirmed: 'You call Abu Bakr the Siddiq and you got his name right.'

His generosity was total. He spent his entire wealth for the sake of Allah — freeing the weak, feeding the poor, supporting the early Muslims at the moment when support meant everything. Umar ibn al-Khattab said of him: 'Abu Bakr was our master and our master freed us' — meaning: Abu Bakr freed Bilal, and through that act, freed the community.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Abu Bakr believes you. He is the Siddiq.' — Reported by Yazid ibn Harun, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: What Abu Bakr left for the ummah
layers.content:
When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, Abu Bakr stood before the community and said the words that steadied Islam at its most fragile moment: 'Whoever worshipped Muhammad — Muhammad is dead. And whoever worshipped Allah — Allah is alive and does not die.'

He was caliph for two years, three months, and ten days. In that time he gathered the Quran, unified the Arabian Peninsula after apostasy threatened to fragment it, and launched the armies that would carry Islam to Persia and the Byzantine lands.

When he was dying he said to Aisha: 'In which garment was the Messenger of Allah washed?' She said: 'In this shirt of his.' He said: 'Wash me in it.' She did so. He died having spent every dirham he earned for the sake of Allah, leaving the treasury with six thousand dirhams — the same amount his daughter Asma reported he began with.

Umar said of him after his death, shaking dust from his grave: 'By Allah, I wish I were a hair on Abu Bakr's chest.'
layers.hadith_ref: Abu Bakr's words at the death of the Prophet ﷺ — narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: What was Abu Bakr's actual given name?

options.text: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafa
Abdullah ibn Uthman
Atiq ibn Abi Bakr
Siddiq ibn Taym

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His name was Abdullah — servant of Allah. Abu Bakr was his kunya, and as-Siddiq was his title. Three names for three dimensions of one man.

quiz.prompt: How much wealth did Abu Bakr have when he became Muslim, and what happened to it?

options.text: Ten thousand dirhams — he kept it for his family
Forty thousand dirhams — he spent it all freeing and strengthening Muslims
Twenty thousand dirhams — he gave half to the Prophet ﷺ
Sixty thousand dirhams — he used it to build the first masjid

quiz.citation: Usama ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, reported in Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Forty thousand became five thousand by the time he reached Madina. The rest became Bilal's freedom, Ammar's safety, and the survival of the early Muslim community.

quiz.prompt: What did Asma bint Abi Bakr cut in two to tie the food bag for the Prophet ﷺ and her father in the cave?

options.text: Her headscarf
Her garment hem
Her belt
Her sleeve

quiz.citation: Narrated in the account of the Hijra, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: She cut her belt to feed the Prophet ﷺ in hiding and earned a title that lasted forever: Dhat an-Nitaqayn — the one with two belts. A small act of love became a name in history.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu Bakr say when he freed Bilal and the Prophet ﷺ mentioned it was a partnership?

options.text: 'He is my gift to you, Messenger of Allah'
'I have already freed him, Messenger of Allah'
'We freed him together, Messenger of Allah'
'Allah freed him through us both'

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not want credit shared. He freed Bilal for Allah alone, not for the Prophet's approval, not for praise. This is the quality of as-Siddiq — sincerity with no audience in mind.

quiz.prompt: What were Abu Bakr's words that steadied the Muslim community immediately after the Prophet ﷺ died?

options.text: 'The Prophet is with Allah now — trust in His mercy'
'Whoever worshipped Muhammad — Muhammad is dead. Whoever worshipped Allah — Allah is alive and does not die'
'Grieve not — the Quran remains with us forever'
'The Prophet foretold this day — we must follow his sunnah'

quiz.scholar_reflection: In the moment of greatest shock, as-Siddiq confirmed the truth again. He had spent his whole life confirming what the Prophet said. In death, he confirmed what Islam means to stand on.

quiz.prompt: Abu Bakr gave everything he had for Islam before being asked. Which of these best describes why that kind of giving is so rare?
quiz.slider_label: How easy is it to give without being asked?

options.text: We wait to see if our giving will be recognised
We give what's comfortable, not what's needed
We haven't found something worth that level of sacrifice
Our certainty in what we believe isn't strong enough yet

quiz.citation: Reflection on the character of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Bakr's giving flowed from certainty. When you are absolutely sure of something, spending for it feels like gain, not loss. His generosity was a measure of his iman, not his character.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ told Abu Bakr 'you have company' when emigrating. Abu Bakr wept at being chosen. What does it mean to be chosen by someone you love for something difficult?
quiz.slider_label: How often do you see difficulty as an honour?

options.text: It means they trust you completely
It means the difficulty matters
It means the relationship is the reward, not the outcome
It means you were prepared without knowing it

quiz.citation: From the account of the Hijra — Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Bakr wept from joy when told he would accompany the Prophet ﷺ into exile and danger. He didn't ask about the risk. The companionship was enough.

quiz.prompt: As-Siddiq's defining quality was confirming the Prophet ﷺ immediately, without needing proof. What makes confirmation without proof so spiritually demanding?
quiz.slider_label: How comfortable are you believing before seeing evidence?

options.text: It requires surrendering your own reasoning
It requires trusting a person more than yourself
It requires accepting that some truths exceed your understanding
It requires having experienced being wrong about your own certainty

quiz.scholar_reflection: Jibril told the Prophet: 'Abu Bakr believes you — he is the Siddiq.' Not because Abu Bakr had no mind, but because his heart preceded his mind in recognising the truth.

quiz.prompt: Abu Bakr died having spent everything he had. When asked about his will, he reportedly said his only wish was to be buried in the shirt of the Prophet ﷺ. What did he value most?
quiz.slider_label: What do you want most to be near at the end?

options.text: The love of the Prophet ﷺ — nearness to him even in death
Simplicity — he had no wealth left to leave anyway
To signal to the ummah what truly mattered
All of the above — these cannot be separated

quiz.citation: Account of Abu Bakr's death — Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He asked to be washed in the Prophet's shirt. That was his inheritance to himself — closeness to the one he loved most. The Siddiq's final act was, like all his acts, a confirmation.

quiz.prompt: Umar said after Abu Bakr's burial: 'I wish I were a hair on Abu Bakr's chest.' What does it mean when the greatest people see themselves as small before other great people?
quiz.slider_label: How does genuine humility differ from false modesty?

options.text: Genuine humility comes from knowing what greatness actually costs
It means they saw something in Abu Bakr that they knew they lacked
The greatest people measure themselves against the best, not the average
True greatness always recognises greater greatness above it

quiz.citation: Umar ibn al-Khattab at the burial of Abu Bakr — Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar, who would go on to conquer half the known world, said he wished to be a hair on Abu Bakr's chest. This is the mark of a soul that knows what piety truly looks like.
